lead: Mass cannot appear or vanish. The continuity equation is that one sentence written in the language of flow: whatever enters a region either leaves it or piles up inside. Engineers use it to find an unknown velocity at a pipe branch, to size a nozzle, to check a flow meter, and to work out how long a tank takes to fill. It is the first of the conservation laws of fluid mechanics, and the only one that needs nothing more than mass and a boundary.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the control volume idea, and Chapter 2.2 for what steady and incompressible mean.

sections.h3: The balance on a control volume

blocks.text: A control volume is a region you draw in space with a boundary you choose. Fluid crosses the boundary; you do not follow individual particles. That fixed window is the natural bookkeeping device for flow.
The mass crossing a surface in one second is the mass flow rate ṁ, in kilograms per second. For a flat area A with fluid of density ρ moving at velocity V straight through it:

blocks.where: ṁ is the mass flow rate, kg/s; ρ the density, kg/m³; A the area, m²; V the average velocity normal to the area, m/s.

blocks.text: The volume flow rate is Q = A V, in m³/s, and ṁ = ρQ. A municipal water connection is quoted in Q; a gas pipeline is quoted in ṁ or in normal cubic metres, because its density changes.
The general statement is short: the rate at which mass inside the control volume changes, plus the net rate at which mass flows out through the boundary, equals zero.

blocks.where: dV is a volume element inside, m³; dA an area element on the boundary, m²; n the outward unit normal; V the velocity vector, m/s. The surface term is positive where fluid leaves.

blocks.text: Two simplifications carry most of the exam marks. In steady flow nothing inside changes with time, so the first term is zero and mass out equals mass in. In incompressible flow ρ is constant and cancels, so volume out equals volume in.
Σ ṁ_in = Σ ṁ_out     and     Σ Q_in = Σ Q_out
blocks.where: the first line holds for steady flow of any fluid; the second holds when the fluid is also incompressible. The sums run over all openings of the control volume.

blocks.text: Shrink the control volume to a small fixed box with sides dx, dy, dz. Let u, v, w be the velocity components in the x, y, z directions, all in m/s.

items: Mass enters the left face at rate ρ u dy dz.
Mass leaves the right face at rate ρ u dy dz + [∂(ρu)/∂x] dx dy dz.
The net outflow in the x direction is therefore [∂(ρu)/∂x] dx dy dz. The y and z faces behave the same way.
The mass stored inside is ρ dx dy dz, changing at the rate (∂ρ/∂t) dx dy dz.
Add the three outflows to the storage term, then divide the whole balance by the volume dx dy dz.

blocks.where: ρ is density, kg/m³; u, v, w the velocity components, m/s; t time, s; x, y, z the coordinates, m. The three space terms together are div(ρV).

blocks.text: For constant density the ρ comes out of every derivative and the whole equation collapses to one line:

blocks.where: this is div V = 0, the incompressible continuity equation. In two dimensions it is ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0.

blocks.text: In polar coordinates (r, θ), with radial velocity v_r and tangential velocity v_θ, the same statement is (1/r)∂(r v_r)/∂r + (1/r)∂v_θ/∂θ = 0.
This equation is why the stream function is useful: any ψ whose derivatives give u and v satisfies div V = 0 automatically, so every such ψ describes a possible incompressible flow.
A stream tube is a bundle of streamlines forming a closed tube. No fluid crosses its walls, so the same mass passes every section of it.

blocks.where: subscripts 1 and 2 are two sections of the same stream tube or pipe; A is the cross-section area, m²; V the average velocity normal to it, m/s; ρ the density, kg/m³.

blocks.text: For a liquid, ρ cancels and A₁V₁ = A₂V₂. A nozzle narrows A, so V rises; a diffuser widens A, so V falls. The same relation sizes the throat of a Venturimeter, which is Unit 3.
At a branching junction in steady flow, the volume flows into the junction add up to the volume flows out. The worked example below is exactly this calculation.

Gases keep the density. Air at 5 bar is roughly five times as dense as air at 1 bar, so a gas main that loses pressure along its length speeds up even when the pipe area does not change; the mass flow stays the same. Water does not behave this way: one kilogram of water fills about one litre at any ordinary pressure, so ρ is treated as constant.

figure.caption: Mass entering and leaving a control volume sets the storage rate. In steady incompressible flow the storage term drops out and the flows simply balance, which is the form used in almost every pipe problem.

spec.title: Mass balance

nodes.label: Steady, incompressible
nodes.note: sum Q in = sum Q out

spec.aria: Mass entering and leaving a control volume fixes the storage rate, and in steady flow the two flows balance.

examples.question: Water flows at 1.5 m/s through a 200 mm diameter pipe. The pipe branches into a 100 mm diameter pipe carrying water at 1.2 m/s and a second branch of 150 mm diameter. The flow is steady and water is incompressible. Find the volume flow rate in each branch and the velocity in the second branch.
steps: Convert diameters to metres and find the three areas, using A = πd²/4, not πd². A₁ = π × 0.200²/4 = 0.031416 m². A₂ = π × 0.100²/4 = 0.007854 m². A₃ = π × 0.150²/4 = 0.017671 m².
Main pipe discharge: Q₁ = A₁V₁ = 0.031416 × 1.5 = 0.047124 m³/s ≈ 0.0471 m³/s.
First branch discharge: Q₂ = A₂V₂ = 0.007854 × 1.2 = 0.009425 m³/s ≈ 0.0094 m³/s.
Steady incompressible balance at the junction: Q₁ = Q₂ + Q₃, so Q₃ = 0.047124 − 0.009425 = 0.037699 m³/s ≈ 0.0377 m³/s.
Velocity in the second branch: V₃ = Q₃/A₃ = 0.037699 / 0.017671 = 2.133 m/s ≈ 2.13 m/s.
Check: 0.009425 + 0.037699 = 0.047124 m³/s, which matches the main pipe.
examples.answer: The second branch carries 0.0377 m³/s at a velocity of about 2.13 m/s.
examples.check:
import math
d1, v1 = 0.200, 1.5
d2, v2 = 0.100, 1.2
d3 = 0.150
A1 = math.pi * d1**2 / 4
A2 = math.pi * d2**2 / 4
A3 = math.pi * d3**2 / 4
Q1 = A1 * v1
Q2 = A2 * v2
Q3 = Q1 - Q2
V3 = Q3 / A3
print(round(Q1, 4))
print(round(Q2, 4))
print(round(Q3, 4))
print(round(V3, 2))

traps: Diameter is not radius. A 200 mm pipe has A = π × 0.200²/4 = 0.0314 m², not π × 0.200². Squaring the diameter without dividing by 4 is the most common lost mark.
Do not drop ρ when the fluid is a gas. A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ is for constant density only; for air or natural gas write ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂.
At a junction, add volume flows only when the same fluid flows in all the pipes. Mixing two different liquids needs a mass balance, not a Q balance.
div V = 0 does not mean the velocity is constant. It means the velocity field has no source or sink; the velocity can still rise in a nozzle.
For a tank that is filling or emptying, the storage term is not zero, so A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ fails. Use ṁ_in − ṁ_out = d(mass inside)/dt.

quiz.q: State the continuity equation for steady flow of an incompressible fluid through a single pipe of varying area.
quiz.a: A₁V₁ = A₂V₂, that is, Q is the same at every section, where A is the cross-section area in m² and V the average velocity normal to it in m/s.

quiz.q: Why does the velocity of water increase when it passes through a nozzle?
quiz.a: The mass flow rate is fixed. For constant density, Q = AV is fixed, so a smaller area A forces a larger velocity V. The fluid accelerates because pressure energy converts into kinetic energy.

quiz.q: Water flows at 2 m/s in a 150 mm diameter pipe that reduces to 75 mm diameter. Find the velocity in the smaller section.
quiz.a: V₂ = V₁(A₁/A₂) = V₁(d₁/d₂)² = 2 × (150/75)² = 2 × 4 = 8 m/s. The area falls to one quarter, so the velocity rises four times.

quiz.q: A gas of density 2 kg/m³ flows at 10 m/s through a 300 mm diameter pipe. Find the mass flow rate.
A tank is being filled through one pipe while water leaves through a hole in the bottom. Explain why A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ cannot be used to relate the two.
quiz.a: The flow is unsteady, so mass inside the tank is changing. The correct balance is ṁ_in − ṁ_out = d(mass inside)/dt. The storage term is not zero, and A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ is only the steady form.

quiz.q: A pipeline carries air and the pressure falls along its length while the area stays constant. Will the velocity stay constant? Justify using the continuity equation.
quiz.a: No. The mass flow ρAV is constant, and A is constant, so ρV is constant. As pressure falls, density ρ falls, so V must rise. The gas speeds up along the pipe.

beyond: Not for the exam. In computational fluid dynamics the continuity equation is solved together with the momentum equations, usually in the conservative form ∂ρ/∂t + div(ρV) = 0, so that shocks and steep density changes are captured without error. Nozzle and diffuser design for compressible flow, met in Unit 3, combines ρAV = constant with the energy and isentropic relations. Weather and ocean models enforce the same balance on a rotating sphere. In biomedical work, continuity explains why a narrowed artery raises the blood speed and lowers the local pressure. Search for: conservative form of the continuity equation, divergence-free velocity field, projection method in CFD.
